m.s: Joshua and the Crossing of the Jordan
o: Heavenly Father, I thank you, because this day is a gift from you. Before I go out to face my tasks, I want to stop before you and acknowledge that, without your help, I cannot take a single step with confidence. You have sustained me this far, and I trust that you will stay with me in the hours ahead.

Lord, you told Joshua to be strong and courageous, because you would be with him wherever he went. Give me that same courage today. There are things before me that intimidate me, decisions I don't know how to make, and paths I cannot yet see clearly. Remove from my heart the fear that paralyzes and the haste that blinds, and teach me to move forward one step at a time, with my eyes on you. Thank you, Lord, for the promises of your Word, which are firm as a rock and hold me up when my emotions change.

Help me to meditate on your Word throughout the day, to remember your promises when doubt comes, and to obey you even when I don't understand everything. May my words be kind, my hands ready to serve, and my heart at rest in the knowledge that you go before me. Keep me from all harm and lead me to do your will with joy. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: After forty years in the wilderness, the people of Israel finally arrived at the edge of the Jordan, facing the land God had promised them. Moses was already dead, and leadership was now in Joshua's hands. It was no small task: before him lay a river in flood and, beyond it, fortified cities.

God spoke to Joshua with words of encouragement: be strong and courageous, do not tremble and do not be afraid, for the LORD his God would be with him wherever he went. He also reminded him that the Book of the Law must not depart from his mouth, but that he must meditate on it day and night in order to obey it.

The time to cross arrived. The Bible tells us that the Jordan overflows its banks throughout the whole time of harvest, which means it was not an easy moment to cross. Yet Joshua ordered the priests carrying the ark of the covenant to go ahead first. And when the priests' feet touched the edge of the water, the waters flowing from upstream stopped and stood up in a heap, a great distance away, while those flowing down toward the Salt Sea were completely cut off.

Before the crossing, Joshua had sent officers through the camp so the people would prepare, and had reminded them that in three days they would cross the Jordan to possess the land. It was a time of preparation and waiting, during which everyone had to look to the Lord and not to the height of the waters.

The people crossed on dry ground, opposite Jericho, and the priests stood firm in the middle of the Jordan until the whole nation had finished crossing. God did not open the way before they took the first step of faith; He opened it when they dared to move forward trusting in His word.
m.c: May the God who was with Joshua go with you today. Go out with a steady heart, knowing that every step is covered by His presence and care. He will open the way just in time, and His peace will accompany you until evening.
m: So often we want to see the whole road before we move. We want the river to be dry before we set a foot on the bank. But Joshua's story shows us that God often opens the way when He sees us moving forward in trust of what He has already told us.

Notice the order of events. First came the promise: I will be with you. Then came obedience: the priests walked toward the water. And only then did the miracle come: the river stopped. If they had waited for the Jordan to dry up by itself, they would still be on the bank. Faith is not feeling secure; it is obeying God even while the river keeps flowing.

Today you may have your own Jordan: a conversation waiting to happen, a job that seems hard, a family problem, or a decision you have put off. You don't need to settle the whole year in a single morning. Ask yourself what the next step is that God has already shown you, and take it. It might be asking forgiveness, making a phone call, organizing your day with order, or simply praying before you begin.

And don't forget the counsel God gave Joshua: meditate on His Word. Before this morning is over, read quietly the verse that touched your heart and carry it with you, perhaps written on a piece of paper. When worry comes, repeat it. Be strong and take courage, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.

o: Lord and my God, at the end of this day I come to give you thanks. Thank you for the air I have breathed, for the bread on my table, for the people you placed in my path, and for every moment I felt your hand upon me. Even in the hard hours, you sustained me and did not let me fall.

I thank you because you are the God who delivers and saves, the One who shuts the mouths of lions when we trust in you. Forgive me if today I doubted or let myself be carried away by fear. I now give you the worries I still carry in my heart, the words I should have kept quiet, and the things I could not finish. You know each of them, and I lay them all in your hands. Thank you also for the chance to serve you, for the health I have had, and for the home that welcomes me when I return, where I can breathe and rest with you.

Watch tonight over my family and those I love. Give me quiet rest, free of anxiety, and wake me tomorrow with a thankful heart. Teach me to be always joyful, to pray without ceasing, and to give thanks in all circumstances, for this is your will for me in Christ Jesus. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: Daniel was an elderly man who had served faithfully in the kingdom of Babylon, and then in that of the Medes and Persians. King Darius esteemed him so highly that he planned to set him over the whole kingdom. This stirred up the jealousy of other governors, who looked for a reason to accuse him, but found no fault in his conduct.

So they said to one another that they could only accuse him in connection with the law of his God. They got the king to sign a decree forbidding prayer to any god or man, except the king, for thirty days. Whoever disobeyed would be thrown into the lions' den.

Daniel learned that the decree had been signed. Even so, he went home, opened the windows of his upper room facing Jerusalem, and knelt three times a day to pray and give thanks to his God, just as he had done before. His enemies saw him and reported him. The king, deeply distressed, tried to rescue him until sundown, but the law could not be changed. Daniel was thrown into the den, and the king told him that his God, whom he served continually, would deliver him.

It is remarkable that the king, who was bound by the law, did not sleep that night. He spent the night fasting and would not have entertainment brought to him. In this way the story ends by showing that Daniel's God is a living God, enduring forever, whose kingdom will never be destroyed.

At dawn, Darius hurried to the den and called out to Daniel in an anguished voice. Daniel answered that his God had sent His angel and shut the lions' mouths, because he had been found innocent before Him. The king was overjoyed and ordered him brought out, and no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.
t.c: As you close this day, give to God everything that has weighed on your shoulders. He has cared for you through the day and will watch over your sleep through the night. Rest in peace and wake up thankful, for His faithfulness is new every morning.
m: Daniel's story teaches us that gratitude and faithfulness can stay firm even when everything around seems threatening. Daniel did not pray in secret or stop giving thanks to God out of fear of the consequences. He simply followed his usual custom, and that constancy was his strength.

Notice that Daniel gave thanks before he saw the deliverance. His prayer did not depend on everything going well. This is a great lesson for the end of this day. Perhaps things did not go as you thought, perhaps there was tension or weariness, but there is always something to give thanks for: life, health, a friend, today's bread, the grace of Christ. Every sincere act of gratitude strengthens trust.

Paul wrote to the Thessalonians to be always joyful, to pray without ceasing, and to give thanks in all circumstances. He did not say to give thanks for everything that happens to us, but in everything, that is, in the midst of every circumstance, because God remains present. Tonight, before sleeping, make a simple list of three good things you received today and thank God for them out loud.

Then give to God the lions that still prowl around you: that financial worry, that difficult relationship, that doubt about the future. The same God who shut the lions' mouths for Daniel can keep you. Lie down in peace, knowing that the Lord does not sleep and that He cares for His own.
